title: Deadly force: It's a case of `lose, lose' when police take extreme action to end a violent situation
article: Rick Parent is an expert on police shootings. He came within a hair's breadth of killing an armed man following a high speed chase.
He is now pursuing a doctorate, and studies the phenomenon of police shootings.
Any deadly shooting incident creates many victims, not the least of whom are the involved police officers, said Parent, a 21-year veteran, and member of the Delta, B.C. police.
"It's a sad tragedy. It's a lose-lose situation for everybody -- the deceased, their family, the officer -- everybody realizes they lose in a shooting."
Through interviews across North America, his focus has been in the area of "suicide by cop" incidents.

Shootings by police fall into two main categories, said Parent. Sixty per cent of people who are killed are in the commission an indictable offence. Most of the remaining incidents are "victim precipitated shootings" that involve people who are often suffering from mental disorders, substance abuse, or are on a suicide quest.

Parent says officers killing a person in the line of duty are probably 10 times more likely to leave policing. Some will quit high- risk assignments; there can be flashbacks, nightmares, post traumatic stress, and family or work-related disorders are not uncommon.
"Anytime a police officer is involved in a shooting incident it is probably the most significant event in their career . . . probably in their life," said Parent.

"It's also an event that flies in the face of what police are taught to do . . . throughout their career they spend a vast majority of their time helping people. They want to save people and they want to make things better." When police make this judgment call, "they are making the situation better because if not they would die, or some other party would die, but the cost is high . . ."
The catalyst for Parent's research was his own brush with death.

It happened following a high-speed chase with an armed man who had escaped an emergency response team. Police shot out the tires on the suspect's vehicle. Parent approached the felon's car, smashed the driver's window with his flashlight and pointed his gun into the vehicle.
The suspect's life was spared when he made no move to aim his shotgun at the officer.

"I knew he could kill me . . . he had the shotgun, and he was only a few feet away from me. At the same time I had a gun literally inches from his face . . . it's pointed right at his head. I knew that was the time when I could take a life. It all happened so fast.
"In hindsight, everything worked out great. He didn't point his gun at me and he didn't shoot and I didn't have to kill anybody."
Parent did, however, feel negative emotions in the aftermath, and he found a lack of literature on the subject to help him. It's a gap he's working to fill.
A Saskatchewan police officer was not so fortunate.

The officer, who wishes to remain anonymous, is still haunted by the fact he killed a man. Recognizing that it is his sworn duty to protect, he still finds it hard to remove the human element from such a responsibility -- and his action.
"I was in a position in which the choices I faced were shoot or be killed . . . I have to live with it every day.

"A police officer is a person. A person who has a family and responsibilities. Friends and family rely on his or her mental health. After an incident of lethal force magnitude, a person's mental health is challenged due to the pressures that accompany it.

"In my personal search to deal with this incident, a wise man told me, life is a gift and it is up to you what you do with it. On that day in question you made the decision to save your gift of life."

Fewer than 10 people are killed annually in shoot-outs by the approximately 55,000 police in Canada. Parent's research found 35 fatal shootings across the three prairie provinces over the last two decades, and 51 people were killed by police in B.C. over the same period.
In Saskatchewan, there have been eight fatal shootings by police in the last decade.

Last week, police from the Saskatoon city and RCMP forces were involved in the shooting death of 33-year-old Keldon McMillan, following a high-speed chase east of the city. Moments before he died, McMillan fatally shot a police dog.
McMillan's death was the third fatal shoot-out involving Saskatchewan police in five weeks. It was the first time in 19 years a Saskatoon police officer was involved in a fatal shooting.

Police have access to professional counselling services, but everyone deals with the situation differently. Although some police services have policies requiring mandatory leave for those involved in a shooting, an immediate return to active duty where the officer can be amongst his peers is becoming accepted.
"No one wants to compel someone to take leave if in fact they cope better by coming back to work," said Saskatoon Const. Grant Obst, president of the Canadian Police Association.

"Just from what I know in the more current realm, many officers would rather come back to work where they have a chance to discuss the situation with the closest thing that can understand -- and that would be other police officers."
Contrary to anecdotal evidence, there is no tendency to suicide among the officers who have killed someone, according to Parent.

Saskatchewan police are trained in the use of force, but while there is a model, they are told there is no standardized response to situations requiring force. Responses can vary depending on an officer's perception of the situation and can involve an escalation from dialogue, to defensive techniques ranging from chemical sprays to blunt force and deadly force. The hope is always for de- escalation.

"In order for an officer to use deadly force, the situation must be grave," said Sgt. Lorne Constantinoff, Saskatoon training officer. "The officer concludes that his or her life, or the lives of other individuals are in danger.

"What you are trying to do is cause cessation of activity. The need must be so great that if the person loses his life as a result of you trying to cease his activity, that loss of life is inconsequential. That's how grave the circumstances must be."
Constantinoff is the firearms instructor for Saskatoon and served as the chief provincial firearms instructor from 1992-95.

Police officers undergo rigorous training in use of force scenarios both in their training at the Saskatchewan Police College in Regina during a "street tactics course" and in a closely-matched program in Saskatoon.

Officers must recertify their firearms training annually. At the same time, they review concepts related to use of force. Saskatoon police are provided with ample ammunition and opportunity to practise their skills on the range.
"The officer dedication (to use of force training) within our service . . . is exceptional," said Constantinoff.
Police use of force -- including deadly force -- is governed by the Criminal Code of Canada.
Parent's research indicates racism is not a factor in police shootings.

"With the issue of racism, what I have found with my Ph.D is that there is nothing to really substantiate it, especially in the last 10 years. Policing is a lot more multicultural now than ever before. We have multicultural police officers. We have women in policing, which we rarely had in the past. We have a lot of training in multiculturalism, which we never had in the past. The issue of prejudice and racism is really unsubstantiated for the most part. There may be the odd isolated case, but I think that has been taken and hijacked by political interest groups and by people with hidden agendas," said Parent.

"What I have found is that most officers are white who kill white people. It's rare that you can say a white officer went out and systematically killed a black person. In fact, you are getting the opposite, and you are getting multicultural officers killing white people, so racism had really nothing to do with it."

Deadly force incidents by police were also the focus for a masters thesis by Saskatoon Sgt. Grant Foster. Foster, who elected not to comment at this time, interviewed 17 police officers who shot and killed in the line of duty. He observed it is important to realize the police are not the sole participants in deadly-force encounters, and society must take some responsibility for the incidents. He said participants felt damned if they do and damned if they don't in such incidents.

Parent was unable to comment directly on the circumstances surrounding recent fatality shooting near Saskatoon, but said having more officers present during a shooting may reduce their aftermath stress levels by allowing them to marginalize their individual participation.
Witnessing the police service dog killed in front of them may have changed the dynamics of the standoff for officers as well, he said.

"It's one thing to say \`I'm going to shoot you.' There's another thing to actually pull out a gun and there's a third level and now we've pointed the gun at you. A fourth level is actually to take someone's life; whether it is a dog or a person it doesn't matter.

"Even a backup person will realize logically that the buttons have been pushed to the fourth level and this person means business. They are going to kill somebody. If they have killed an animal, they're going to kill someone else."
Ultimately, what must be realized, say officers, is that the police are responding to a threat of deadly force when they act.

"The question quite often comes up, \`is there anything that could have been done to prevent the application of deadly force so that this person was not shot?' The answer to that question is yes. There is something that someone could have done and that someone is the individual themselves," said Constantinoff.
"The situation is always dictated by the individual."
